sources.context: Vanity Fair cover story built from a month of interviews in spring 2022, promoting Persuasion and Cha Cha Real Smooth. It is the first time Johnson spoke at length about the Fifty Shades production; the writer frames it as an unburdening after years of promotional silence, and she balances it with praise for E.L. James. The Hitchcock material is Johnson’s view of her grandmother’s experience; the underlying account is Tippi Hedren’s, and Vanity Fair supplies the characterization of Hitchcock’s conduct. Contains testimony from Richard E. Grant, Riley Keough, Melanie Griffith, Tippi Hedren, Cooper Raiff and Olivia Colman (S23–S27). In the Fifty Shades section the writer, not Johnson, links the contract to “the binding agreement that Hitchcock used to ruin her grandmother’s career”; that comparison is Vanity Fair’s and is not used. The same section pairs the fear-and-protection lines with “both Jamie and I were treated really well” and her praise of James.

claims.inference: Research-stage search result.
claims.alternative: A response may exist or appear; absence of a found response is not evidence that none exists.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck for any statement by E.L. James or her representatives before each release; if one appears, add it beside Johnson’s account and re-weigh C07/C69.

claims.claim: In 2024 she said that with Fifty Shades “the author was extremely precious about words, clothing, anything, everything,” and that there was “no room for being expressive or discovering what is present in that real moment that you’re capturing. It’s contrived.”
claims.inference: Her grievance is contrivance and lost expression, quoted in her own words rather than the draft’s harsher paraphrase.
claims.alternative: Artist rhetoric after a public fallout; still her framing.

claims.claim: She founded TeaTime Pictures in 2019 with former Netflix development executive Ro Donnelly; interviewed at its office in late February 2020, she told Marie Claire, “For a long time, I’d do a movie and have no say.”
claims.inference: A costly, long-term structural choice made so her work would not be turned into something it wasn’t.
claims.alternative: Control and autonomy (Eight) or career strategy (Three) also explain founding a production company; many stars do.

claims.claim: She told Marie Claire (2020), “I could go into something, and it’ll be one thing, and then it comes out as a totally different thing.”
claims.inference: The same grievance as Fifty Shades, generalized; Marie Claire notes she had denied displeasure with Fifty Shades (C147).
claims.alternative: Ordinary actor frustration; career control (Eight/Three) also explains it.

claims.claim: The High Note screenwriter Flora Greeson says Johnson told her, “I don’t want this character apologizing in every scene. That’s not what Maggie does.”
claims.inference: A concrete behavioral instance: she defends a character’s right to be openly emotional without apologizing for it.
claims.alternative: Also fits ordinary actorly instinct or a feminist reading of the role; one anecdote.

claims.claim: In a Bustle Q&A published March 5, 2024, answering a question about the film’s nasty reviews, she said she “probably will never do anything like it again because I don’t make sense in that world,” and “That’s why I have my own company. In a movie like that, I have no say about anything.”
claims.inference: Her grievance is the familiar one (a project becoming something else); her stated plans about such films change with the moment.
claims.alternative: “Along for the ride” is Nine-like passivity; the reversal could be mood, press context or a joke.

claims.claim: In June 2025 she told the Los Angeles Times that “with ‘Madame Web,’ it started out as something and turned into something else. And I was just sort of along for the ride at that point.”
claims.inference: The same grievance a year later.
claims.alternative: “Along for the ride” is also the best Nine evidence (C106).

claims.claim: Interpretation: across a decade her grievance is that what reached the screen stopped being what she signed up to make.
claims.inference: Synthesizes C07, C75, C28, C76.
claims.alternative: Control (Eight) or career strategy (Three) also explain the complaint.

claims.claim: Discussing author involvement in adaptations, she said in 2024, “It’s also about control and feeling powerful, and that’s not what art is.” The article notes this criticizes an author’s control, not her own.
claims.inference: Said about someone else’s control; it does not settle her own motive, which the article now states.
claims.alternative: She may want control for herself; her stated remedy is her own company (C139).

claims.claim: She described the TeaTime set to Vogue in 2026 as “womb-like” and “a protective maternal space,” because “I’ve had experiences where people feel forgotten or lost or not taken care of or not seen on set or just undervalued, and I don’t like anyone to feel that way.”
claims.inference: What she builds when she has power is a place where people are seen; she values the experience of making over output.
claims.alternative: Protectiveness and caretaking also fit Two and Six; this is promotional framing of her company.

claims.claim: She and Cooper Raiff deferred their fees on Cha Cha Real Smooth because the financiers couldn’t afford the costs of making a movie during COVID (Vanity Fair, 2022).
claims.inference: Costly, sustained effort for small, specific projects she loves; confirmed by several named collaborators.
claims.alternative: Ambition and career strategy explain producing; collaborators are grateful and promotional.

claims.claim: Daddio writer-director Christy Hall says Johnson suggested Sean Penn and that “Within 48 hours, Dakota told me Sean wanted to talk to me”; Penn’s AP account says she knocked on his door with the script.
claims.inference: Two named witnesses confirm her hands-on producing.
claims.alternative: Grateful collaborators in release promotion.

claims.claim: In spring 2026 she produced and starred in Alice Rohrwacher’s Three Incestuous Sisters, shot on Stromboli and in Rome with costars including Saoirse Ronan; Vogue (September 2026) says the film is due in 2027. No distributor release date had been announced as of October 8, 2026.
claims.inference: Current-accuracy facts; not needed for the personality argument.
claims.alternative: Release dates and credits shift.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck the release date and reception at each refresh; the Stromboli shoot is the evidence that matters, not the release.

claims.claim: She said, “When people feel valued and safe to explore their minds, magic happens,” and “The way that it went with Three Sisters, I would be okay if that was the last movie I make” (Vogue, 2026).
claims.inference: Values the experience of making over output; safety framed as the condition for free exploration.
claims.alternative: Promotional enthusiasm for her own production.

claims.claim: In 2017, responding to tabloid claims that she and Jamie Dornan couldn’t stand each other and were having an affair, she told Vogue, “We hate each other and we’re having an affair, so everybody’s right. How about that?”
claims.inference: Her press put-ons predate the viral 2019 persona (C141).
claims.alternative: A joke; says little about motive on its own.

claims.claim: On The Ellen DeGeneres Show (aired November 27, 2019), when DeGeneres said she hadn’t been invited to Johnson’s 30th birthday party, Johnson answered, “Actually, no. That’s not the truth, Ellen. You were invited.”
claims.inference: A truthful on-air correction, not a put-on: she declined to go along with a false story about herself even when it was played as a joke. The edit stage moved it out of the put-ons and uses it as their contrast.
claims.alternative: Reads as Eight-like assertion or simple honesty; a Nine reading would expect her to let it slide. One moment; do not overload it. Quote only speaker-unambiguous lines. Her tone is not described: the captions do not record it, and the earlier “laughing” descriptor was dropped at the repair stage.

claims.claim: Asked about the Ellen exchange in 2024 by an interviewer who praised it (“There’s a special place in heaven for you being on the Ellen show… It was a really winning moment.”), she said, “It will haunt me.”
claims.inference: Wry weariness at being defined by a meme, answering praise; no regret or feud is implied.
claims.alternative: Meaning uncertain; humor.

claims.claim: In January 2021 she told Fallon, “I actually didn’t even know that they were in there,” describing the limes as set dressing.
claims.inference: First version of the limes story.
claims.alternative: Comic register.

claims.claim: In December 2021 she said she saw the bowl of limes while filming (“I love them”) and that an allergy test “a few weeks later” showed she is allergic.
claims.inference: Second, different version; the shifting account is the observation.
claims.alternative: Do not treat either version as the factual sequence.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the limes confession is itself a bit and changes between tellings.
claims.inference: Compares C49/C50 with C51.
claims.alternative: Talk-show craft; says little about core motive.

claims.claim: Vogue (2026) reports that, according to Johnson, her posture toward the press is less a “bit” than a survival tactic; she imagines a journalist asking whether she bites the bed during sex and says she fucks around with the press and has fun doing it “because the other side is fucking with me.”
claims.inference: Her own framing of the put-ons as defense.
claims.alternative: Fits counterphobic testing or a child raised in tabloids as well as any type.

claims.claim: The Ringer’s Jodi Walker (February 14, 2024), an admirer who loves Johnson “wholeheartedly and fearfully,” wrote that “She will lie—but only at the most unexpected times” and that Johnson lacks the concern other public figures carry “about telling the exact truth about what she thinks and feels in the exact moment.”
claims.inference: An admiring, non-promotional commentator treats her candor as genuine; the edit stage corrected the draft’s framing of Walker as a skeptic.
claims.alternative: Affectionate commentary, not evidence of motive; the commercial-incentive point is this profile’s own inference (C144).

claims.claim: James Foley, director of Fifty Shades Darker and Freed, told Vogue in 2017, “She has a very sensitive bullshit meter, so if she does something that is the least bit unreal she just stops herself.”
claims.inference: A collaborator’s 2017 observation of aversion to the false, predating her later candid persona.
claims.alternative: Director promoting his film; quoted in a flattering profile.

claims.claim: Alessandro Michele, a friend of more than a decade and Gucci’s designer (Vogue, 2017), calls her “the most natural person I have met in this business” (Vogue, 2026); Wikipedia says she has been named a Gucci brand ambassador.
claims.inference: Friend’s testimony converging with Foley, with his commercial tie disclosed so readers can discount it.
claims.alternative: Interested witness with a business relationship; not independent of S01.

claims.claim: Interpretation: Foley’s 2017 testimony matters most because it predates the candid persona.
claims.inference: Dating argument against “authentic is only her later brand.”
claims.alternative: Still one director’s promotional remark.

claims.claim: Interpretation: her line runs between a bit everyone can see is a game and a faked feeling; she has stated the first half herself (C11), the second half is inferred.
claims.inference: Labeled in the article as half her own rule, half inference; tested against the Fifty Shades years (C147–C149).
claims.alternative: She may simply enjoy lying; the limes confession itself shifted.

claims.claim: In late February 2020, talking about the COVID-19 scare, she told Marie Claire, “I’m constantly thinking about the state of the world right now. It keeps me up at night, all night, every night,” and “My brain goes to crazy dark places with it.”
claims.inference: Real, recurring anxiety, mostly tied to exposure (performing, press scrutiny) and world events.
claims.alternative: Supports a Six reading; also fits social anxiety, a childhood under tabloid scrutiny, and depression. Do not use the L’Officiel “Terrified of what happens to me” line as self-reported fear: in context it is a joke about other actors.

claims.claim: On The Tonight Show in January 2021 she said, “When I come on your show, I get really nervous, and I laugh and then cry most of the time,” and described a panic attack before a singing scene in Our Friend as “like extreme flight mode.”
claims.inference: Stage fright and panic in performance settings.
claims.alternative: Common performance anxiety; comic register.

claims.claim: Before the 2026 press tour she said, “everything is watched, and now everyone is a spy, and everyone is the press” (Vogue podcast).
claims.inference: Vigilance about exposure.
claims.alternative: Fame explains it for anyone.

claims.claim: In 2026 she told Vogue, within minutes of meeting the writer, “I am obsessed with people not knowing where I am or what I’m doing,” adding, “I’m far too porous and sensitive and present. I don’t—I can’t deal.”
claims.inference: Privacy, consistent with 2015.
claims.alternative: Fame and a tabloid childhood explain privacy without any type.

claims.claim: In 2017 she said, “A few years ago, I was fighting, waiting for someone to give me a chance. I’m a pretty sensitive person, and when I don’t feel protected, I tend to close right up. But when I feel safe, I think I can do anything.”
claims.inference: Safety supplied by trusted collaborators, then the ability to act: the shape Six theory predicts. Counted as Six evidence at the edit stage; it does not discriminate for Four.
claims.alternative: A Four also needs safety before opening up; on its own the line fits both readings.

claims.claim: Explaining “The blood of the covenant is thicker than the water of the womb” in 2024, she said it means “the connections with people you choose are more solid than the connections to the people you’re actually born to.”
claims.inference: Loyalty to a chosen circle, voiced by someone who grew up among seven half-siblings (C59).
claims.alternative: Loyalty is central to the Six alternative; her large blended family explains it circumstantially.

claims.claim: In a jokey 2024 Bustle Q&A she called herself “a real sucker. I would be the first one to join a cult,” and, asked which cult, named any that promised “this will make you a better person for other people.” In a separate answer, after the interviewer called her persona anti-authoritarian, she said, “I am a very defiant person. If somebody tells me I can’t do something, I am shaking, even if I had no interest in doing that thing.”
claims.inference: Two separate joking answers; the authority contrast was the interviewer’s. Read literally, reflexive defiance looks counterphobic.
claims.alternative: She flagged exaggeration in this interview; Fours resisting definition, Eights and Sevens predict the same defiance.

claims.claim: Interpretation: read literally the defiance looks counterphobic, but it comes from an interview she flagged as exaggerated and other types predict it, so it does not discriminate.
claims.inference: Reclassifies the defiance as non-discriminating instead of a Six signature left unanswered.
claims.alternative: A Six reader may still weight it; the article keeps it in the Six case.

claims.claim: Describing what she and Maggie Gyllenhaal let go of on The Lost Daughter, which she tied to turning 30, she said, “She kind of was my shepherd in that way. It’s almost like we both unshackled ourselves from something,” and named it: “this fear of when you have the potential to do things, but you’re just like, is that going to be okay?” (2021).
claims.inference: Doubt-and-permission language plus a trusted guide: the best single passage for the Six case. Quoted in source order at the repair stage (the shepherd line comes first; the fear is what they “unshackled” from).
claims.alternative: She frames the fear as an obstacle to becoming her fullest self, which a Four reading can absorb.

claims.claim: On Materialists she “felt like I was in such good hands, I could just relax into that role” (2025).
claims.inference: She can cede control when she trusts the filmmaker.
claims.alternative: Fits Nine ease or Six trust in a good authority; argues against a pure Eight reading.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the Six case (anxiety, vigilance, loyalty, ambivalence toward authority, trusted guide) is why confidence is medium.
claims.inference: Summarizes C20–C23, C29, C45, C90–C92.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the discriminator between Four and Six is the relation between her fear and her grievance. She names fear readily, and it is always circumstantial (fame, the contract at 23, explicit scenes, singing, press scrutiny, not working); her grievance, told across 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025, is never that she was misled or left unprotected but that the work stopped being the work she signed up to make. In the one passage where fear and grievance meet (Vanity Fair, 2022) she separates them herself: the contract “was scary,” she and Dornan “had to… protect each other,” and yet “both Jamie and I were treated really well,” while the complaint remains which movie got made.
claims.inference: A Six’s injury fuses fear and grievance (an authority who misled or exposed her); a Four’s injury is the loss of what was distinctive or true in the work. Hers takes the second shape even where the first was available.
claims.alternative: Her incentive to protect working relationships (“I don’t want to hurt anyone’s career”) could be suppressing a trust grievance; the independent accounts (Taylor-Johnson’s “her vision versus mine,” James’s “I had to fight for a lot of things”) describe a fight over vision rather than a betrayal, which limits that reading without excluding it.
claims.review_trigger: Reopen if she describes any production conflict as being misled or left unprotected, or if a collaborator describes her complaint that way.

claims.claim: Recalling learning at 10 that the Easter Bunny didn’t exist, she said in 2022, “But if I could, I would still believe in it now. Maybe that’s why I make movies and why I want to make movies forever and ever. It makes things feel a little bit more safe.”
claims.inference: In this line belief and moviemaking serve safety; the edit stage moved it from the Four side to the Six case.
claims.alternative: A light anecdote about enchantment; a Four could also treat make-believe as refuge.

claims.claim: She said of choosing projects in 2020, “I really don’t have a method, and I don’t want one… It’s very intuitive and emotional.”
claims.inference: Decisions run on feeling and taste rather than systems, guidance or rules.
claims.alternative: A Seven or Nine could also resist method; producers often say this in interviews.

claims.claim: She said in 2024, “I think I just find rules and some structure really ridiculous, silly and stupid,” and told Vogue in 2026, “Rules are really tough for me.”
claims.inference: Resistance to rules corroborated across two outlets and years.
claims.alternative: Counterphobic Six (reflexive defiance of authority), Eight (autonomy) and Nine (accommodate, then quietly do your own thing) all fit parts of this.

claims.claim: She said in 2024, “Everyone who makes decisions is afraid. They want to do the safe thing, and the safe thing is really boring.”
claims.inference: She disdains safety-seeking and control in creative decisions, the opposite of what a security-first motive would defend.
claims.alternative: Common artist rhetoric during a bad box-office moment; also fits Eight anti-control sentiment.

claims.claim: She has said she has struggled with depression “since I was 15 or 14” and “I am in a lot of therapy” (Marie Claire, 2020), adding, “But I’ve learned to find it beautiful because I feel the world”; she is “always trying to navigate that in an honest and safe way” (Vanity Fair, 2022); Vogue (2026) reports various modalities of therapy; she received the Hope for Depression Research Foundation’s HOPE Award in November 2023.
claims.inference: First-person mental-health history with the professional and personal support she credits in all three sources. Not used as type evidence.
claims.alternative: Depression can mimic Four melancholy; the article states it is not type evidence (C154). Wikipedia’s unsourced rehabilitation claim is not used.

claims.claim: Of a scarab tattoo, a symbol of rebirth, she said in 2022, “I think that’s been me forever,” and, reading that Roe v. Wade was likely to be overturned, “if I didn’t try and apply great meaning to little things, I honestly don’t think I’d make it.”
claims.inference: A habit of symbolic meaning-making; a lean toward Four, not a separation.
claims.alternative: The scarab line sits in the same breath as her therapy and depression remarks; a Six can anchor in belief too.

claims.claim: She said she felt like her Lost Daughter character, Nina, “so hungry and so thirsty for something else and to be seen—to not just be the hot girl on the beach,” adding, “I feel like that in my career a lot” (2021).
claims.inference: Names being seen accurately, beyond surface image, as a career-long hunger and as the basis of trust.
claims.alternative: Awards-campaign talk about a role; actors routinely identify with characters. The specificity (“the hot girl on the beach,” trust built on not being seen) is the evidence.

claims.claim: She said she trusted Gyllenhaal “because I knew that she knows what it feels like to not be seen” (2021).
claims.inference: The trust behind the Six-case “shepherd” line rests on being seen.
claims.alternative: The same answer adds “She knows what it feels like to not be handled with grace and with care,” which is protection language a Six reading can claim.

claims.claim: Richard E. Grant said in 2022 that “having seen her on that infamous Ellen DeGeneres interview, you know that she takes no prisoners.”
claims.inference: A forceful public presence, partly derived from the Ellen clip (Grant says so).
claims.alternative: Fits Eight; much of it is costar warmth in promotional contexts.

claims.claim: Anne Hathaway, her Verity costar, said in 2026, “She’s actually very cozy and lovable, but she has, unmistakably, very, very powerful jungle cat energy.”
claims.inference: Forceful presence, with warmth.
claims.alternative: Costar promoting the same film.

claims.claim: In 2017 she said that after two years of exposure she went into “this weird K-hole of feeling so scared of people” and became “shut off to strangers, even cold. That’s not my nature. I prefer to be tender”; Vogue reported in 2017 that tender is her favorite word and tattooed on her forearm.
claims.inference: Volunteered vulnerability, with the fear clause restored at the edit stage; dated to 2017.
claims.alternative: Fear of people also feeds the Six case; an Eight can admit softness privately, but these are public admissions.

claims.claim: She said in 2018, as relayed from Entertainment Weekly, “I’m a very porous person and I absorb a lot of people’s feelings.”
claims.inference: Volunteered permeability, repeated as “porous” in 2026.
claims.alternative: Secondary relay of EW.

claims.claim: She said in 2024, “I can be out at my house and not see or speak to another human for days on end, and I feel wonderful.”
claims.inference: Withdrawal and rest are restorative for her.
claims.alternative: Strongest support for a Nine or withdrawn reading; depression and exhausting schedules also explain it.

claims.claim: She calls her home life “Just low-key” (Vogue, 2026).
claims.inference: Restorative quiet.
claims.alternative: Fits Nine; also ordinary.

claims.claim: On Madame Web she was “just sort of along for the ride” (2025).
claims.inference: Nine-like passivity in one project.
claims.alternative: Could be resignation on a studio film.

claims.claim: In 2017 she said, “I think I’m a little bit heartbroken all the time, even when I’m in a happy relationship. I don’t do casual very well, and my feelings, even the good ones, get so intense that they hurt.”
claims.inference: Longing and heightened feeling as a standing condition rather than a reaction to events, stated nine years apart.
claims.alternative: Depression (C04) and an actor’s trained emotional access can produce the same language.

claims.claim: Her friend Talia Bernstein says, “She’s sillier than most people know… I’ve been at so many small gatherings with her where she’s putting on a dance or changing into a costume…. She likes to laugh” (Vogue, 2026).
claims.inference: A strong playful, mischievous streak that coexists with the melancholy self-description.
claims.alternative: Fits Seven; the melancholy-only Four stereotype does not predict it.

claims.claim: On a 2026 Vogue podcast she joked that she and Jennifer Lawrence “could be the ultimate internet trolls if we, A, had the time and, B, the interest.”
claims.inference: Mischief.
claims.alternative: A joke.

claims.claim: Asked about motherhood in 2024, she said, “I really want to experience everything that life has to offer,” and a few sentences later, “There’s so much to eat up and learn and grow from and experience and feel. That includes all the pain and the suffering and feeling so helpless about the world.”
claims.inference: Unlike a Seven’s appetite, hers explicitly embraces suffering and self-reproach as part of what she wants to feel.
claims.alternative: Read alone, “experience everything” is Seven language; the second half is what separates it.

claims.claim: She said in 2017, “The stories I want to tell, the characters I want to play, don’t typically exist in huge, commercial box-office movies… But this is a business.”
claims.inference: Commercial calculation that supports a Three reading; the same sentence names non-commercial taste.
claims.alternative: Supports a Three or practical-careerist reading of some choices; tempers the purist image.

claims.claim: In March 2024 she said she probably would never do anything like Madame Web again; in June 2025, “There’s no part of me that’s like, ‘Oh, I’ll never do that again’ to anything. I’ve done even tiny movies that didn’t do well. Who cares?”
claims.inference: Stated plans change with the moment; the shrug at films that “didn’t do well” cuts against an image-protecting Three reading (C155) and against reputational distancing as the whole story (C140).
claims.alternative: Press context or a joke.

claims.claim: Interpretation: her anxiety is high for a Four, and depression can mimic Four melancholy.
claims.inference: Counterevidence and a diagnosis-vs-personality caution.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Sources from outside her promotional circle are Sam Taylor-Johnson (S35), E.L. James (S44), The Ringer (S38) and two February 2024 critics’ essays (S51, S52); none is a collaborator’s critical account of her as a producer, and none speaks to her private motives.
claims.inference: Source-limit statement.
claims.alternative: None.
claims.review_trigger: Reopen if a collaborator, crew member or financier gives a critical first-hand account of a TeaTime production or of her conduct on set.

claims.claim: The July 2026 Vogue interview was timed to Verity, a thriller costarring Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett; the film opened in North America on the weekend of October 2–4, 2026 and took in $32.6 million in its first weekend (AFP, citing Exhibitor Relations) despite weak reviews; Johnson was 36.
claims.inference: Dated context only; not needed for the argument.
claims.alternative: Release details shift.
claims.review_trigger: Update the gross only if the article cites it; the first-weekend figure is an initial industry report and final totals may differ.

claims.claim: Vogue reports that when filming ends on a project with “this really intense connection to the material” and everyone goes home, she finds it “shattering,” and she said, “I’ve felt that sort of heartbreak I don’t even know how many times now in my life… It’s like leaving summer camp. It’s so devastating. And I don’t know how much more heartbreak my heart can handle.”
claims.inference: Intense, recurring grief at the end of a shoot she is deeply connected to (Vogue’s condition, kept at the repair stage); she presents it as a thing that happens on set, not as unique to her.
claims.alternative: Common among actors; depression also colors it.

claims.claim: Vogue says the Stromboli shoot was the kind of thing she joined the industry to be part of: “a safe container full of artists feeling free.”
claims.inference: Vogue’s phrase, attributed as such.
claims.alternative: The writer’s framing.

claims.claim: Interpretation: wrap grief is common and a Six could mourn a lost secure group; what is specific is how often she says it recurs and what ends.
claims.inference: Replaces the draft’s unsupported “most actors” contrast.
claims.alternative: Actors commonly grieve wrap; the Six reading of a lost secure group is stated in the passage.

claims.claim: She said in July 2026, “Maybe spending a little bit more time just existing as a human is what I’ll be doing.”
claims.inference: Dated closing statement.
claims.alternative: Plans change.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck at each refresh against her announced projects; the sentence is dated to July 2026 and is no longer the article’s closing line.

claims.claim: In the same Bustle interview she said, “Truly, but I know I’ve exaggerated in this interview, and you can tell that I’m exaggerating because you see my face. If it’s written down, it’s hard.”
claims.inference: Discloses her own caveat where Bustle lines first carry weight; no discriminator rests on a single Bustle line without corroboration.
claims.alternative: The caveat may itself be a joke; it applies to tone, not to every line.

claims.claim: Interpretation: faking a feeling is hard for her by her own account; the Fifty Shades years show she can hold back the whole truth.
claims.inference: Narrows the thesis to what C15, C67, C08 and C171 support: during promotion she withheld the fight but stated pride and mixed feelings she later repeated.
claims.alternative: She may simply enjoy performance; see C148.

claims.claim: In high school she lived mostly with her mother and her stepfather, Antonio Banderas (Vanity Fair, 2022: “then married to Antonio Banderas”; Wikipedia: her former stepfather).
claims.inference: Family context for a blended upbringing; no causal personality claim is drawn.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Asked in 2024 whether constantly moving and being the new kid was weird, she said, “I didn’t find it weird because it was what was normal to me.”
claims.inference: Her accounts of the same childhood shift with the venue, a counterpoint to the darker 2017 and 2026 tellings.
claims.alternative: Both can be true at once; venue and question shape the answer.

claims.claim: Per Wikipedia, her film debut was Crazy in Alabama (1999), beside her mother and half-sister Stella Banderas, directed by Antonio Banderas; in 2006 she was the first second-generation Miss Golden Globe.
claims.inference: Early industry access; attributed to Wikipedia in the prose. No causal personality claim.
claims.alternative: Tertiary source; the facts are uncontroversial filmography and award records.

claims.claim: She applied to one college, Juilliard, and was not accepted (Wikipedia); she told Vogue in 2017, “Juilliard and I mutually agreed that it wouldn’t work out.”
claims.inference: A deadpan line laid over a disappointment, years before the limes.
claims.alternative: One joke; says little about motive on its own.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the 2017 and 2018 Fifty Shades praise dates from the years she later said she could not talk about truthfully.
claims.inference: Flags that “different is what I’m about” is a promotional-period line.
claims.alternative: The praise may have been sincere; see C148.

claims.claim: Asked about regret in 2022, she said, “If I had known at the time that’s what it was going to be like, I don’t think anyone would’ve done it. It would’ve been like, ‘Oh, this is psychotic.’ But no, I don’t regret it.”
claims.inference: Restores the full no-regret passage behind the Vanity Fair headline.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Interpretation: as she tells it, the Fifty Shades grievance is not about credit or money.
claims.inference: Reads C07, C69 and C74. The repair stage dropped “danger”: her 2022 account includes fear and protection (C165, C166), which the discriminator section now weighs.
claims.alternative: Her account; James has not responded (C70).

claims.claim: Madame Web, a superhero film, opened in February 2024; Wikipedia calls it “critically and commercially unsuccessful.”
claims.inference: Orients readers to the film and its reception; The Ringer calls it a superhero movie.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Interpretation: an Eight or Three might also found a company; her stated remedy, “That’s why I have my own company” (Bustle, 2024), is a say of her own.
claims.inference: Concedes that founding TeaTime does not discriminate.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the timing of her grievances also fits reputational distancing; Fifty Shades grossed over $1 billion and she shrugs at her flops, which fit that story poorly without ruling it out.
claims.inference: Names and tests the reputational-distancing alternative.
claims.alternative: Fifty Shades was critically mocked, so distancing from it is still possible.

claims.claim: L’Officiel (2024) says the Ellen interview “set the internet on fire in 2019”; Vogue (2026) dates her deadpan press reputation to the Ellen clip and the AD video.
claims.inference: Dates the viral persona so readers can check that the 2017 put-on and Foley’s 2017 remark come before it.
claims.alternative: The Ringer traces press-junket mischief to 2015; the viral reputation is what dates to 2019.

claims.claim: In the same Ellen exchange, after recalling being teased about it on the show the year before, Johnson said, “But I did invite you, and you didn’t come,” and DeGeneres conceded, “No, I think I do remember I was invited.”
claims.inference: Context from the same transcript for why she pushed back.
claims.alternative: Captions are unlabeled; attribution rests on sequence (“you gave me a bunch of [BLEEP] about not inviting you. But I did invite you”) and contemporaneous descriptions.

claims.claim: The Ringer describes the Ellen exchange as responding to teasing “with legitimate truth.”
claims.inference: A second account supports classing the clip as a truthful correction.
claims.alternative: Commentary.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the commercial value of her candor is this profile’s caveat, not Walker’s argument.
claims.inference: Labels the incentive point as the author’s own.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Interpretation: she has stated the first half of the bit/feeling line herself (the ridiculous-situation rule); the second half is inferred.
claims.inference: Corrects the draft’s “not a rule she has stated.”
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Marie Claire noted in 2020, in a parenthetical with no date or wording, that she “has denied reports that she was displeased with the Fifty Shades films.” The dated printed statements that fit are Vogue UK, reported January 5, 2016 (“I’m proud of Fifty Shades of Grey. I don’t need to distance myself from that,” S47) and Vogue, January 13, 2017, where the writer answered “Not so” and she said, “I’m truly proud of it” (S08).
claims.inference: The parenthetical is Marie Claire’s summary; the two printed statements are what the record can date. Neither denies that the production was a fight; both affirm pride and refuse distance.
claims.alternative: A denial with other wording may exist in an unindexed outlet; search of 2015–2020 coverage on 2026-10-07 and 2026-10-08 found none.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the pride she stated during promotion (2016, 2017, 2018) is the pride she repeated in 2022 (“I’m proud of what we made ultimately”); what she withheld until 2022 was the fight, not her feeling about the result.
claims.inference: Weighs C67 against C08, C66 and C171: the 2017 answers admit recurring regret (“It comes in waves”) and state pride; the 2022 account adds the fight.
claims.alternative: A Three or a loyal Six would also hold a promotional line; the reading is inference from her later account, and the denial Marie Claire mentions (C147) is unknown.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the supportable claim is that faking it is hard for her, she can manage a version of it when a release depends on it, and eventually she tells the fight, though not all of it.
claims.inference: “Not all of it” rests on her 2022 line that “There are things that I still cannot say” (C168).
claims.alternative: See C148.

claims.claim: Interpretation: protection from collaborators, then the freedom to act, is the shape Six theory predicts.
claims.inference: Concedes that the safety framing does not discriminate.
claims.alternative: A Four needs safety too.

claims.claim: Interpretation: on her talk of safety alone, the Six reading would win.
claims.inference: States plainly that the Four lead rests on the grievance and being-seen evidence (C95, C16, C100).
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Interpretation: her High Note script note defended a character’s right not to apologize for herself.
claims.inference: A named collaborator’s behavioral anecdote used as expression evidence.
claims.alternative: Ordinary actorly instinct; one anecdote.

claims.claim: She told the AP in 2024, “This notion of executives, not necessarily creative people, deciding what is going to work in an artistic sense doesn’t actually make sense to me at all.”
claims.inference: Corroborates the expression framing in a different outlet from Bustle in the same year.
claims.alternative: Producer promotion; also fits distrust of authority (Six).

claims.claim: Interpretation: her depression and therapy are care for a medical condition and are not used as type evidence.
claims.inference: Implements the standard’s caution against treating a mood disorder as personality.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the Three reading has support (commercial frankness, years on message), but she punctures her image in public (doesn’t “make sense” in the superhero world, shrugs at flops, would accept Three Incestuous Sisters as her last film).
claims.inference: An explicit Three discriminator, with C39 and C147 as the evidence for it.
claims.alternative: Public self-deprecation can itself be image management; promotional settings.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the dated printed statements (January 2016, January 2017) affirm pride and refuse to distance her from the films; neither denies that the production was contested. They therefore show a promotional line held for years, not a false denial of the fight, and do not move the reading toward a Three’s image management or a loyal Six’s discipline on their own.
claims.inference: Holding back a grievance while promoting is common to every type under contract; what is type-relevant is that the feeling she stated (pride in something “different”) is the one she kept.
claims.alternative: If a dated statement in which she flatly denied any conflict surfaces, the Three or loyal-Six reading of those years strengthens.
claims.review_trigger: Reopen if a 2015–2021 statement denying the fight itself is found.

claims.claim: Interpretation: a collaborator’s account of a TeaTime production gone wrong could move the read; a fight framed as being misled or left unprotected points toward Six, one framed as the work made false toward Four.
claims.inference: Names an observable reopen signal for the contested typing.
claims.alternative: None.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck at each refresh, on the release of Three Incestuous Sisters, and whenever a non-promotional long-form account or collaborator testimony appears.

claims.claim: Interpretation: what she mourns at wrap is the connection to the material inside the safe set, and by her own account it has happened more times than she can count.
claims.inference: Vogue ties the grief to films with “this really intense connection to the material” (C116); “more times than she can count” paraphrases “I don’t even know how many times.”
claims.alternative: Common among actors; a Six could mourn the secure group itself (C118).

claims.claim: Dakota Johnson is an American actress (Wikipedia) and producer (TeaTime; AP, Vogue), best known for the Fifty Shades of Grey films (Wikipedia: her breakthrough; Vogue 2026: “shot her into the stratosphere”).
claims.inference: Orientation for a cold reader.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Of the three-picture contract she signed at 23, after James, by Johnson’s account, scrapped Patrick Marber’s script in anger over Charlie Hunnam’s exit, she told Vanity Fair in 2022, “I was young. I was 23. So it was scary,” then, “It just became something crazy,” she continued.
claims.inference: The stated fear is of being bound by contract to a production that had changed under her; Vanity Fair, not Johnson, adds the Hitchcock-contract comparison, which is not used.
claims.alternative: A 23-year-old signing a three-picture contract would be scared regardless of type; Vanity Fair, not Johnson, links it to Hitchcock’s contract with her grandmother.

claims.claim: In 2022, answering rumors of a feud with Jamie Dornan (“There was never a time when we didn’t get along… he’s like a brother to me”), she said, “We had to really trust each other and protect each other.” Of the more outrageous scenes she said, “We were doing the weirdest things for years, and we needed to be a team: ‘We’re not doing that,’ or ‘You can’t do that camera angle.’”
claims.inference: The protection is mutual and bodily, in explicit scenes; it is said in defense of the Dornan friendship, not as a complaint about an authority.
claims.alternative: The trust line answers rumors of a feud with Dornan; refusing camera angles is also ordinary boundary-setting on intimate scenes, and fits an expressive or Eight reading as well.

claims.claim: Interpretation: read alone, the 2022 fear and protection lines (C165, C166) are compatible with a Six’s story; read in their own passage, where she adds that “both Jamie and I were treated really well” and that James “was always kind to me,” the fear attaches to the contract and the scenes, not to a betrayal of trust.
claims.inference: Concedes the counterevidence the verifier raised (verify-02) before weighing it.
claims.alternative: A Six can also say she was treated well and still feel unsafe; the counterweight is that she never names an unmet need for protection as the injury, in any outlet, across 2016–2025.

claims.claim: In the same 2022 passage she said, “There are things that I still cannot say because I don’t want to hurt anyone’s career and I don’t want to damage anybody’s reputation, but both Jamie and I were treated really well.”
claims.inference: She declines to frame the set as mistreatment of the two actors, and says she is still withholding details to protect others’ careers; supports “not all of it” (C149).
claims.alternative: “Treated really well” is also what a promotionally careful or loyal speaker would say; the withheld details are unknown.

claims.claim: Interpretation: when she sums up her troubled films and the industry across 2020, 2024 and 2025, the complaint is lost expression and sameness: a film “comes out as a totally different thing” (2020); “no room for being expressive… It’s contrived” (2024); “Everyone who makes decisions is afraid. They want to do the safe thing, and the safe thing is really boring” (2024); Madame Web “turned into something else” (2025); “creative decisions are made by a committee… they remake the same things… humans don’t want that. They want fresh” (2025).
claims.inference: Repeats C75, C74 and C76 as a pattern across three outlets and five years.
claims.alternative: Expression vocabulary is industry-standard; all are promotional interviews.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the Four reading leads on the content of her self-definition (difference, being seen, feeling), on the content of her grievances (lost expression), and on how she overrides fear (by claiming a vision and choosing exposure); the Six reading stays live on the volume of her fear and support language. The discriminator separates on content, not on how much safety she needs.
claims.inference: Weighs C165–C168 against C169, C152 and C153; the reason the call stays at medium confidence.
claims.alternative: A reader weighting her most detailed account over her summaries could favor Six.
claims.review_trigger: Check at each refresh whether new first-person accounts of fear credit trusted people and preparation (Six) or freedom to feel and express (Four).

claims.claim: Asked by Glamour UK in early 2017 whether she ever wished she hadn’t made the Fifty Shades films, she said, “It comes in waves,” and, in the same answer, “I do feel proud of it.”
claims.inference: During promotion she admitted recurring regret alongside pride, so the promotion years show withholding of the fight rather than a faked, unmixed feeling.
claims.alternative: Relayed by a fashion site, original not opened; the question framing is the relay’s. Still a promotional answer.

claims.claim: E.L. James told the AP in February 2015, days before the first film opened, that she was “thinking about the readers” and “I had to fight for a lot of things really hard. And I did.”
claims.inference: James’s own framing of the adaptation fight: advocacy for her readers. It corroborates that there were fights and gives her motive in her words; it predates and does not respond to Johnson’s or Taylor-Johnson’s accounts.
claims.alternative: Promotional interview; “fight” here is her word for creative advocacy, not an admission of conflict with Johnson.

claims.claim: Interpretation: by her own later account she held a promotional line that was not the whole truth, but the feeling she stated then (pride, answering reports she despised the films, Vogue 2017) is the one she kept.
claims.inference: Connects C67 to C08: the printed 2017 denial affirmed pride, which she repeated in 2022.
claims.alternative: Pride in a finished product is compatible with any type; the inference concerns consistency, not motive.

claims.claim: In her first British Vogue interview (February 2016 issue, reported January 5, 2016), eleven months after the first film opened, she said, “I’m proud of Fifty Shades of Grey. I don’t need to distance myself from that.”
claims.inference: A dated, printed statement affirming pride and refusing distance; it is the earliest match for the denial Marie Claire mentions. It does not address whether the production was a fight.
claims.alternative: Promotional obligation under a three-picture contract would produce the same line from any type.

claims.claim: In the same 2016 interview she said, “This industry is fucking brutal,” “No matter how tough you are, sometimes there’s the feeling of not being wanted. It’s absurd and cutthroat,” and, “Whenever I have downtime, I’m unsure that I will ever work again. I don’t know what it is, but it’s a definite thing that happens to me.”
claims.inference: Recurring insecurity about being wanted and employed; it fits a Six’s anticipatory doubt and a Three’s dependence on being chosen, and the “not being wanted” frame also fits a Four’s sense of being overlooked. Counterevidence to be weighed, not explained away.
claims.alternative: Actors of every type report this fear; it is not discriminating on its own.

claims.claim: On Hot Ones (June 12, 2025), asked why Hollywood is risk-averse, she said, “I think it’s hard when creative decisions are made by a committee. And it’s hard when creative decisions are made by people who don’t even really watch movies or like know anything about them. And that tends to be what’s occurring a lot,” and that when something does well “studios want to keep that going, so they remake the same things… but humans don’t want that. They want fresh, they want to feel new things, experience new things, see new things.”
claims.inference: Her industry critique names sameness and committee as the enemy and “fresh… feel new things” as the good; the same shape as her 2020, 2024 and 2025 grievances.
claims.alternative: This is a common complaint among actor-producers and does not by itself establish motive.

claims.claim: In 2024 she told L’Officiel, “All of the stuff I’m interested in making is really different, and it’s unique and it’s very forward in whatever it is,” that getting Daddio made “took a lot of fighting to get that made,” and, “People are just so afraid, and I’m like, why? What’s going to happen if you do something brave?… Everyone who makes decisions is afraid. They want to do the safe thing, and the safe thing is really boring.” She also said, “The people who run streaming platforms don’t trust creative people or artists to know what’s going to work.”
claims.inference: She defines her own taste by difference and treats other people’s fear and safety-seeking as the obstacle; the “don’t trust creative people” line shows she can frame the problem as distrust, but the remedy she names is bravery and difference, not reassurance.
claims.alternative: A counterphobic Six also mocks others’ caution; the discriminating part is that her stated good is difference and feeling, not courage for its own sake.

claims.claim: In July 2025 she told Variety she would direct a small feature written with Vanessa Burghardt: “I’ve always felt that I’m not ready to direct a feature… I don’t have the confidence, but, with her, I feel very protective and I know her very well,” and, “I can see this world, so I just won’t let anybody else do it. That’s the real answer.”
claims.inference: She states a lack of confidence and overrides it by claiming a vision and ownership of the material, not by assembling backup or certainty; the protectiveness is toward a collaborator, not a request for protection.
claims.alternative: A Six can also act out of loyalty to a vulnerable collaborator; the vision claim (“I can see this world”) is what tilts this toward Four.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck whether the film was made and how she described directing it.

claims.claim: In the same July 2025 interview she said, “I can’t waste time on toxic sets anymore, or in situations that are not fun or fulfilling or healthy,” and “I don’t want to face people who are not willing to collaborate.”
claims.inference: Her stated condition for working is a healthy, collaborative set; this is where the safety language of 2017 and 2026 lands in practice.
claims.alternative: Any established actor-producer with leverage says this; it fits Six (security) and Four (a container for feeling) equally.

claims.claim: Accepting the HOPE Award in November 2023, she said, “Most of the time as you can probably tell, I speak about depression or anxiety in a very self-deprecating way,” “I sometimes find it easier to look it in the eyes if I mask it in comedy,” and “Covering my pain or anxiety with comedy has become a lifelong tool… Because, sometimes if I don’t laugh, I will cry.”
claims.inference: Her own account of the deadpan: comedy as a way to look at pain rather than avoid it. It explains the press persona without any type and is compatible with Four (pain owned), Seven (pain reframed) and Six (anxiety managed).
claims.alternative: A speech at an advocacy event is a performance with its own incentives; the wording is Hola’s transcription.

claims.claim: In the same speech she described a low day a few weeks earlier: her partner asked, “Are you really struggling?”, she said no, he pointed to her Cats T-shirt, and “it turns out, I really was struggling. But that moment lifted me up and pulled me out of it.”
claims.inference: Being noticed and named by a trusted person lifts her; this is reassurance-seeking evidence that keeps the Six reading alive and also fits a Four’s wish to be seen.
claims.alternative: The anecdote is about depression, a medical condition, and is not type evidence on its own.

claims.claim: Interpretation: in Vanity Fair’s 2022 passage, the fear attaches to the contract (“I was 23. So it was scary”) and the protection to the outrageous scenes (“we needed to be a team: ‘We’re not doing that,’ or ‘You can’t do that camera angle.’”), while in the same breath she says “both Jamie and I were treated really well” and James “was always kind to me” and that she is “grateful she wanted me to be in those movies.” The grievance that survives those concessions is which movie got made: “the takes of the movie that Erika wanted to make, and then… the takes of the movie that we wanted to make.”
claims.inference: Her fear and her grievance are separable in her own telling; the grievance is about expression, not protection. This is the core of the Four-versus-Six discriminator.
claims.alternative: She says she is still withholding details to protect careers, so a trust grievance could exist unspoken; the independent accounts (S35, S44) describe a fight over vision, not a betrayal.

claims.claim: Two critics writing during the February 2024 Madame Web press tour, from outside her promotional circle, read her the same way: The Hollywood Reporter’s Richard Newby called her press manner “often notably deadpan and brutally honest,” and The Daily Beast’s Laura Bradley wrote, “I don’t think she hates Madame Web so much as the brainless machine that made it.”
claims.inference: Outside readers locate her anger in the machinery, which matches her own framing; they are not collaborators and do not speak to motive.
claims.alternative: Both are defending her against a pile-on and are not adversarial sources.

claims.claim: Three days before the first Fifty Shades film opened in February 2015, she told The Telegraph (via PTI), “Now everyone’s the press. I feel fame is perforated: it can be glorious but it can completely destroy a human too.”
claims.inference: The “everyone is the press” frame appears in 2015 and again in 2026 (“now everyone is a spy, and everyone is the press”); vigilance toward exposure is a constant, not a late development.
claims.alternative: A child of two famous parents whose addiction struggles were tabloid material has circumstantial reasons for this; it does not settle type.

claims.claim: Interpretation: when she overrides fear, the override is a claim of vision or a choice of exposure (directing because “I can see this world”; the “big naked movies” because “when I’m interested in something, I want to know so much about it”; singing the Our Friend scene with the camera behind her), not the securing of certainty, allies or rules. She rejects method and rules outright.
claims.inference: Six theory predicts fear managed through preparation, authority and alliance; Four theory predicts fear tolerated for the sake of feeling and being seen. Her stated overrides fit the second.
claims.alternative: A counterphobic Six also charges at fear; the difference is that she frames the charge as curiosity and expression, not as defiance of the fear itself.

claims.claim: In 2022 she said, “I’m a sexual person, and when I’m interested in something, I want to know so much about it,” and “That’s why I did those big naked movies,” and, of playing Nina in The Lost Daughter, “I was letting go of how I allowed others to look at me.”
claims.inference: Her account of why she took Fifty Shades is appetite for experience and curiosity, and her account of The Lost Daughter is release from others’ gaze; neither is a security motive.
claims.alternative: A retrospective rationale given seven years later; the 2015 Telegraph relay records doubts she had at the time (not opened).

claims.claim: In 2021 she said of her career, “how can it be better than this? I want something deeper and darker, more real and more honest,” after describing Nina as “so hungry and so thirsty for something else and to be seen” and adding, “I feel like that in my career a lot.”
claims.inference: What she wants more of is depth, darkness and honesty, the Four’s stated goods, not safety or success.
claims.alternative: Awards-season framing for a prestige film invites this vocabulary.

claims.claim: Interpretation: Type Two is a partial alternative. She calls her sets “womb-like” and “a protective maternal space,” says she does not like anyone to feel “forgotten or lost or not taken care of or not seen,” feels “very protective” of a collaborator, calls herself “porous,” and jokes she would join a cult that promised to make her “a better person for other people.”
claims.inference: Her care is real and recurring, but she never describes her worth as being needed; she describes it as being seen and being different, and the care she gives is explicitly the care she wanted on sets where she felt unseen.
claims.alternative: A Two with a Four-ish presentation would also say “not seen”; the record lacks the Two’s characteristic resentment at being unappreciated.

claims.claim: At Cannes in May 2025 she said, “Some professionals who run studios don’t feel the desire to make things that are different or risky… or scary or dangerous or raw and real and human and messy,” that pushing against this is “a constant fight. But we are fighters. We hustle,” and that “So much of why I wanted to start a production company and make my own movies is because I want more from this industry.”
claims.inference: Her list of what the industry refuses is a Four’s list of goods (different, raw, real, human, messy); the stated reason for TeaTime is wanting more, not wanting safety.
claims.alternative: A promotional talk for a producing banner invites exactly this rhetoric; it corroborates the 2020, 2024 and 2025 grievance pattern rather than proving motive.

claims.claim: In the same talk she said, “I found myself as an actor, a few times, showing up to the premiere of a movie to see it the first time… That is not what I thought we were making,” and described TeaTime’s set culture as “very much a no asshole policy.”
claims.inference: The grievance in its plainest form: the finished film differing from the film she thought she was making. The no-asshole policy is a set-culture rule for others, consistent with the protective sets she describes in 2026 (C26).
claims.alternative: A rule protecting the set fits a Six’s security-building as well as a Four’s container for feeling; the premiere line is what carries the discriminator.

type_hypothesis.against: Real evidence resists Type Four and keeps Six alive. (1) Fear and anxiety recur across the whole record: fame “can completely destroy a human too” (2015, C186); “Whenever I have downtime, I’m unsure that I will ever work again… the feeling of not being wanted” (2016, C177); “feeling so scared of people” after two years of exposure (2017, C35); “when I don’t feel protected, I tend to close right up” (2017, C20); COVID-era dread that kept her up “all night, every night” (2020, C21); stage fright and a panic attack before a singing scene (2021, C90); “this fear of when you have the potential to do things, but you’re just like, is that going to be okay?” and Gyllenhaal as her “shepherd” (2021, C45); “everyone is a spy, and everyone is the press” (2026, C91); “I don’t have the confidence” to direct (2025, C180). (2) Her safety language is Six-shaped on its own: protection from collaborators who “give me a chance” precedes the freedom to act (C20, C150, C151); moviemaking “makes things feel a little bit more safe” (2022, C98); she relaxes “in such good hands” (2025, C29); a partner noticing her low day “pulled me out of it” (2023, C183); she values chosen-family loyalty (C23) and works only on sets that are “healthy” and collaborative (C181). (3) Her fullest Fifty Shades account (2022) contains fear and mutual protection: the contract at 23 “was scary” (C165) and she and Dornan “had to really trust each other and protect each other” and act as “a team” in refusing camera angles (C166); read alone those lines tell a Six’s story (C167). (4) The Bustle defiance (“I am shaking, even if I had no interest”) reads counterphobic if taken literally, though it comes from an interview she flagged as exaggerated (C22, C93, C129). (5) Three: “this is a business” (C39); years on message for Fifty Shades (C176, C08, C66, C171); grievances voiced only after films finish or flop (C140); a Gucci ambassadorship and a bankable candor The Ringer prices (C85, C144). (6) Two: womb-like sets, “protective maternal space,” porousness, protectiveness toward Burghardt (C193). (7) Eight for the Ellen correction, “takes no prisoners,” “jungle cat energy,” defiance and her own company (C09, C34, C102, C139); Nine for days alone, “Just low-key,” “along for the ride” (C32, C105, C106); Seven for play, costumes, trolling and comedy as a “lifelong tool” (C33, C109, C11, C182). (8) Incentives and circumstance: “authentic,” “different” and “brave” are industry vocabulary; a rootless, tabloid-exposed childhood (C02, C03, C62) explains privacy, vigilance and not belonging without any type; lifelong depression (C04) can mimic Four melancholy and is not used as evidence; nearly all testimony is from friends and collaborators in promotional pieces, and the outside voices (S35, S38, S44, S51, S52) do not speak to motive (C113).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Counterphobic Type Six is the strongest rival. The volume of fear language is the Six’s: doubt about being wanted or working again (C177), fear of people and of exposure (C35, C91, C186), anticipatory dread (C21), stage fright (C90), the contract that “was scary” (C165), the question “is that going to be okay?” (C45) and the admitted lack of confidence to direct (C180). Her remedies are the Six’s too: a trusted guide (“shepherd,” C45; “such good hands,” C29), mutual protection (“protect each other,” C166), a partner who notices (C183), chosen family (C23), a protected set (C26, C117, C181), rules for others while rejecting rules for herself, and reflexive defiance of anyone who says she cannot (C22). Her industry critique can be framed as distrust (“don’t trust creative people or artists,” C179; “people who don’t even really watch movies,” C178). On this reading, TeaTime is a security structure, the deadpan is vigilance (“a survival tactic,” C84) and the Four-sounding talk of difference is the counterphobic Six’s refusal to be told what to do. Type Three is the second rival (commercial frankness, years on message, timing of grievances: C39, C176, C140, C155). Type Two (C193), Eight (C09, C34, C139), Nine (C32, C105, C106) and Seven (C11, C33, C182) each explain a visible piece and fail on her standing intensity of feeling (C18), her appetite for “the pain and the suffering” (C44) and her repeated self-definition by difference (C06, C08, C179).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: The relation between her fear and her grievance (C95, C184, C190), tested against the strongest Six evidence rather than around it. She names fear freely, and every named fear is circumstantial: fame (2015, 2017), the three-picture contract at 23 (2022), explicit scenes (2022), singing (2021), press scrutiny (2026), not working (2016). A Six’s injury fuses fear and grievance: the authority who misled her or left her exposed. In the one passage where her fear and her grievance meet (Vanity Fair, 2022) she separates them herself: the contract “was scary,” she and Dornan “had to really trust each other and protect each other” in “the weirdest things,” and yet “both Jamie and I were treated really well” and James “was always kind to me,” while the complaint that survives is which movie got made, “the takes of the movie that Erika wanted to make, and then… the movie that we wanted to make” (C69, C168, C184). Two independent accounts describe the same fight as a clash of visions, not a betrayal: Taylor-Johnson’s “Her vision versus mine” (2017, C72) and James’s “I had to fight for a lot of things really hard” for readers (2015, C172). Across outlets and years the grievance keeps that shape: a film “comes out as a totally different thing” (2020, C75); “no room for being expressive… It’s contrived” (2024, C74); “the safe thing is really boring” (2024, C179); Madame Web “turned into something else” (2025, C76); “they remake the same things… humans don’t want that. They want fresh” (2025, C178). Her self-definition has the same content: “different is what I’m about” (2017, C08), Fincher’s “did something different” as the best thing anyone ever said to her (2022, C06), “to be seen—to not just be the hot girl on the beach” and “deeper and darker, more real and more honest” (2021, C16, C192), “All of the stuff I’m interested in making is really different” (2024, C179), “I just want to be authentic” when called cool (2026, C14, C53). And when she overrides fear, the override is a vision claim or a choice of exposure, not a securing of certainty: “I don’t have the confidence, but… I can see this world, so I just won’t let anybody else do it” (2025, C180); “when I’m interested in something, I want to know so much about it. That’s why I did those big naked movies” (2022, C191); no method, no rules (C24, C13).
